claims.source: According to previous results (Otwinowski and Nemenman, 2013), the distribution of mutations in terms of maximal promoter activity is peaked at 1, but skewed to the left (Figure 6b). This indicates that about 10% of them yield cells with nearby 50% lower expression.
claims.evidence: Based on data from Otwinowski and Nemenman 2013, shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: For E. coli, the per base mutation rate is 10^-10 mut./bp/gen.
claims.source: For E. coli, where the per base mutation rate is of 10−10 mut./bp/gen. (Lee et al., 2012), this frequency can be estimated in 10−9 (i.e. 0.2 mutants with nearby 50% lower expression per generation in a natural population of 2·108 cells).
claims.evidence: Empirical mutation rate from Lee et al. 2012.

claims.claim: The probability that a duplication and a promoter mutation reducing expression by 50% concur in the same E. coli cell in a generation is 10^-4.
claims.source: Hence, the probability that a duplication and such a mutation concur in the same cell in a generation (duplication after promoter mutation) is of 10−4 (=0.2·10−3/2; i.e., 1 suitable concurrence each 104 generations).
claims.evidence: Calculated from mutation and duplication rates.

claims.claim: At constant 0.13 mM lactose in a highly noisy scenario, the mean selection coefficient is 0.19% when wild-type expression is recovered upon duplication.
claims.source: In particular, at constant 0.13 mM lactose, we obtained a relatively high mean selection coefficient of 0.19% when the wild-type expression is recovered upon duplication (in a highly noisy scenario).
claims.evidence: Calculated from fitness model with gene dosage sharing.

claims.claim: The selection coefficient has to be greater than the duplication deletion rate to ensure fixation.
claims.source: However, the selection coefficient has to be greater than the duplication deletion rate to ensure fixation (Figure 5b); a condition that is not met here.
claims.evidence: Population genetic principle illustrated in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: High deletion rates observed in bacteria protect them from acquiring genetic redundancy.
claims.source: Certainly, the high deletion rates observed in bacteria (Reams et al., 2010) protect them from acquiring genetic redundancy (perhaps, this is why lacZ is not duplicated in E. coli despite this may be beneficial).
claims.evidence: Inference from deletion rate data and observation that lacZ is not duplicated in E. coli.

claims.claim: In some genetic contexts in bacteria, the deletion rate of a lacZ duplicate can be as low as 4.1·10^-4 -/gene/gen.
claims.source: In other local genetic contexts, also in bacteria, the deletion rate of a lacZ duplicate can be as low as 4.1·10−4 -/gene/gen. (Reams et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Empirical data from Reams et al. 2012.

claims.claim: The global fixation probability of lacZ duplication in E. coli is estimated at 3·10^-7.
claims.source: We then estimated a global fixation probability of 3·10−7 (= 2·15·10−4·10−4; Figure 6d; see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: Calculated from mutation rates, duplication rates, and selection coefficients, shown in Figure 6d.

claims.claim: The estimated fixation probability of 3·10^-7 is much higher than 5·10^-9, the fixation probability under hypothetical neutrality.
claims.source: Remarkably, our estimation is much higher than 5·10−9, the fixation probability under hypothetical neutrality (Kimura, 1983).
claims.evidence: Comparison with neutral fixation probability from Kimura 1983.

claims.claim: For Drosophila melanogaster, the per base mutation rate is 5·10^-9 mut./bp/gen.
claims.source: For D. melanogaster, for instance, where the per base mutation rate is of 5·10−9 mut./bp/gen. (Schrider et al., 2013), and complete gene duplications have little impact on fitness (Emerson et al., 2008; note that other genome rearrangements not affecting entire genes are significantly deleterious), we estimated that 0.05 mutants with nearby 50% lower expression and up to 105 duplicants of the gene of interest would be found in the natural population.
claims.evidence: Empirical mutation rate from Schrider et al. 2013.

claims.claim: Complete gene duplications have little impact on fitness in Drosophila melanogaster.
claims.source: For D. melanogaster, for instance, where the per base mutation rate is of 5·10−9 mut./bp/gen. (Schrider et al., 2013), and complete gene duplications have little impact on fitness (Emerson et al., 2008; note that other genome rearrangements not affecting entire genes are significantly deleterious), we estimated that 0.05 mutants with nearby 50% lower expression and up to 105 duplicants of the gene of interest would be found in the natural population.
claims.evidence: Empirical observation from Emerson et al. 2008.

claims.claim: The probability of concurrence of duplication and promoter mutation in Drosophila melanogaster is 2.5·10^-3.
claims.source: Hence, the probability of concurrence in the same organism (duplication after promoter mutation) would be of 2.5·10−3.
claims.evidence: Calculated from mutation and duplication rates for D. melanogaster.

claims.claim: The global fixation probability for duplicates in Drosophila melanogaster is 10^-5.
claims.source: Consequently, the global fixation probability would be of 10−5; again, higher than the one under hypothetical neutrality (Kimura, 1983).
claims.evidence: Calculated from mutation rates, duplication rates, and selection coefficients.

claims.claim: In many cases of duplication, there is no significant increase in total expression comparing duplicates in S. cerevisiae vs. singletons in S. pombe.
claims.source: In many cases of duplication, there is no a significant increase in total expression (e.g. duplicates in Saccharomyces cerevisiae vs. singletons in Schizosaccharomyces pombe; Qian et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Empirical observation from Qian et al. 2010.

claims.claim: The preservation of the ancestral function in the second copy is expected after duplication.
claims.source: In any case, the preservation of the ancestral function in the second copy is expected (DeLuna et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to DeLuna et al. 2008.

claims.claim: E. coli genes fsaA and fsaB are paralogs with 69% sequence similarity coding for fructose-6-phosphate aldolase.
claims.source: In E. coli, for example, genes fsaA and fsaB are paralogs, with high sequence (69%) and functional similarity, coding for a genuine fructose-6-phosphate aldolase (Sánchez-Moreno et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Empirical data from Sánchez-Moreno et al. 2012.

claims.claim: E. coli expresses two redundant gluconokinases encoded in genes gntK and idnK with 51% sequence identity.
claims.source: In particular, E. coli expresses two redundant gluconokinases, encoded in genes gntK and idnK (51% of sequence identity), to face environments in which gluconate is the carbon source due to glucose oxidation (Vivas et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: Empirical data from Vivas et al. 1994.

claims.claim: Gluconate activates the expression of gntK and idnK by inhibiting the transcriptional repressor GntR.
claims.source: Similar to the regulation of lacZ by lactose (Jacob and Monod, 1961), gluconate activates the expression of gntK and idnK by inhibiting the transcriptional repressor GntR (Afroz et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Empirical data from Afroz et al. 2014.

claims.claim: GntR produces bimodal responses as captured in single-cell experiments.
claims.source: Arguably, duplication might have been fixed in this case to cope with gene expression inaccuracies, especially when GntR produces bimodal responses (captured in single-cell experiments; Afroz et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Empirical observation from Afroz et al. 2014.

claims.claim: A significant number of duplicates could be fixed by genetic drift only in complex organisms (higher eukaryotes).
claims.source: On the one hand, a significant number of duplicates could be fixed by genetic drift only in complex organisms (i.e. higher eukaryotes; sector A in Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Conclusion from the comprehensive model shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Fixed duplications by drift would not be stable due to formation-deletion balance and would require accumulation of beneficial mutations or gene relocation for long-term preservation.
claims.source: However, these fixed duplications would not be stable, due to the formation-deletion balance (Reams et al., 2010), and then, for a long-term preservation, they would require the accumulation of beneficial mutations (Han et al., 2009), or the relocation of the second copy in the genome to prevent its deletion (Ranz et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Inference supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: When environmental changes are relatively rapid, only organisms with short generation times (prokaryotes and lower eukaryotes) could fix duplications by positive selection.
claims.source: When the environmental changes were relatively rapid, only organisms with short generation times (i.e., prokaryotes and lower eukaryotes) could fix duplications (sector C in Figure 7; Riehle et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Conclusion from the comprehensive model shown in Figure 7, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Duplications fixed due to rapid environmental changes would be quickly eliminated once the environment changed again.
claims.source: However, such duplications would be quickly eliminated from the population afterwards (once the environment changed again), as the genome rearrangement rates are orders of magnitude higher than the per base mutation rates (Reams et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Inference from comparison of genome rearrangement and mutation rates.

claims.claim: When environmental changes are prolonged, any organism can fix duplications under strong positive selection.
claims.source: By contrast, when a given environmental change were prolonged, any organism, irrespective of its generation time, could fix duplications (sector D in Figure 7; Emerson et al., 2008). In this case, they would be under strong positive selection, and, consequently, they would be preserved for long time.
claims.evidence: Conclusion from the comprehensive model shown in Figure 7, supported by citation.

claims.claim: All organisms could fix duplications by producing more accurate responses without significant environmental changes, provided the gene is noisily expressed and the deletion rate is lower than the selective advantage.
claims.source: Furthermore, all organisms could fix duplications by producing more accurate responses (sector B in Figure 7), without the need of significant environmental changes; provided the gene of interest were noisily expressed (Elowitz et al., 2002; Raser et al., 2004), and the duplication deletion rate were lower than the weak selective advantage.
claims.evidence: Conclusion from the comprehensive model shown in Figure 7, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Weak selective conditions could allow the exploration of novel functions in the very long term.
claims.source: In the very long term, these weak selective conditions could also allow the exploration of novel functions, as they ensure the preservation of duplicates, without invoking fortuitous exploration in the ancestral state (Bergthorsson et al., 2007), and with amplification when the advantage provided by the narrowed novel function were higher than the advantage by noise reduction.
claims.evidence: Speculation about long-term evolutionary consequences, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Gene duplication can be positively selected as an architecture that allows enhancing information transfer in genetic networks.
claims.source: The inherently stochastic nature of gene expression is certainly an evolutionary driver when it is linked to cell fitness to dictate the selection of particular genetic architectures (Batada and Hurst, 2007; Maamar et al., 2007). Our results demonstrate that gene duplication can be positively selected as an architecture that allows enhancing information transfer in genetic networks (i.e. mitigation of expression errors; Rodrigo and Poyatos, 2016).
claims.evidence: Main conclusion of the study, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The genetic robustness observed upon accumulation of genetic redundancy would be more a consequence than a selective trait.
claims.source: Accordingly, the genetic robustness indeed observed upon the accumulation of genetic redundancy (Keane et al., 2014) would be more a consequence than a selective trait (Kafri et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Interpretation of existing observations, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Duplication would be more favorable in scenarios in which intrinsic noise is preponderant.
claims.source: Certainly, by aggregating the responses of two genes, intrinsic fluctuations can be mitigated, but not fluctuations of extrinsic nature. This way, duplication would be more favorable in scenarios in which intrinsic noise is preponderant.
claims.evidence: Logical consequence of the noise buffering mechanism.

claims.claim: Intrinsic noise can be significant when the medium is rich in nutrients, expression levels are low, and no further regulations affect the gene.
claims.source: Intrinsic noise can be significant when the medium is rich in nutrients, the expression levels are low, and no further regulations affect the gene (Swain et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Conditions for intrinsic noise dominance, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Competence in Bacillus is mainly governed by intrinsic noise.
claims.source: For example, competence in Bacillus is mainly governed by intrinsic noise (Maamar et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Example from literature, supported by citation.

claims.claim: A population genetic model with the mean selection coefficient is enough to explain the complex, stochastic evolutionary dynamics of duplication fixation.
claims.source: Moreover, our results highlight that a population genetic model with the mean selection coefficient is enough to explain the complex, stochastic evolutionary dynamics of duplication fixation.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by agreement between theoretical predictions and simulations.

claims.claim: Gene expression level is indicative of the fixation path for duplicates.
claims.source: First, the gene expression level is indicative of the fixation path. The theory requires that gene expression is roughly maintained (i.e. gene dosage sharing, duplicates vs.. singletons), with the aim of minimizing deleterious fitness effects.
claims.evidence: Testable prediction from the theory.

claims.claim: Most formed duplicates would be under strong purifying selection due to the cost of over-expression.
claims.source: This would hold for several fixed duplicates in different organisms (Qian et al., 2010; Gout and Lynch, 2015; Cardoso-Moreira et al., 2016; Lan and Pritchard, 2016), although most of the formed duplicates would be under strong purifying selection due to the cost of over-expression, as already proposed (Lynch and Conery, 2000).
claims.evidence: Inference supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Fixed duplicates showing increased gene expression levels would reflect the effect of genetic drift or positive selection for dosage after prolonged environmental changes.
claims.source: By contrast, those fixed duplicates showing increased gene expression levels would reflect the effect of genetic drift (Lynch and Conery, 2003) or positive selection for dosage after prolonged environmental changes (e.g. the case of flies; Emerson et al., 2008; Cardoso-Moreira et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: Noisy genes are expected to be more duplicable when noise has deleterious fitness effects.
claims.source: Second, noisy genes are expected to be more duplicable (e.g. as it seems to happen in yeast; Lehner (2010); Dong et al., 2011) when noise has deleterious fitness effects.
claims.evidence: Testable prediction supported by citations to yeast data.

claims.claim: TATA box enrichment in cis-regulatory regions of duplicated genes is explained by their association with high plasticity and high gene expression noise.
claims.source: This would explain the TATA box enrichment in the cis-regulatory regions of duplicated genes, as these genetic motifs are associated to high plasticity (i.e. high sensitivity to multiple environmental changes) and high gene expression noise by inducing transcriptional bursts (Blake et al., 2006; Lehner, 2010).
claims.evidence: Explanation of empirical observation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: If noise were beneficial, duplication would not be favored.
claims.source: Note that if noise were beneficial (e.g. as a survival strategy in fluctuating environments; Acar et al., 2008), duplication would not be favored.
claims.evidence: Logical consequence of the theory, with citation to example.

claims.claim: Essential genes would be less duplicable as a consequence of their reduced gene expression noise.
claims.source: Moreover, we might argue that essential genes would be less duplicable (He and Zhang, 2006) as a consequence of their reduced gene expression noise (Batada and Hurst, 2007).
claims.evidence: Inference connecting observations from two cited studies.

claims.claim: Genes under the control of regulatory structures that buffer noise would not be duplicable.
claims.source: Genes under the control of regulatory structures that buffer noise (e.g. negative feedbacks) would not be duplicable either (Warnecke et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Inference supported by citation.

claims.claim: The local genetic context would be highly determinant of the fixation of a duplicate, explaining why some genes are more duplicable than others.
claims.source: Third, the local genetic context would be highly determinant of the fixation of a duplicate (Reams et al., 2012), explaining why some genes are more duplicable than others in scenarios of apparent neutrality (hot spots; Perry et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: Duplicates would be much shorter lived in prokaryotes than in eukaryotes due to differences in duplication deletion rates.
claims.source: Moreover, duplicates would be much shorter lived in prokaryotes than in eukaryotes (Lynch and Conery, 2003), due to the differences of orders of magnitude in the duplication deletion rates.
claims.evidence: Inference from deletion rate data, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The precise experimental determination of molecular rates of gene copy number variation would unveil to what extent natural selection has rivaled random genetic drift to shape complexity.
claims.source: After all, the precise experimental determination of the molecular rates of gene copy number variation would unveil to what extent natural selection has actually rivaled random genetic drift to shape complexity along the course of life history (Rodrigo, 2017).
claims.evidence: Future research direction proposed by the authors.

claims.claim: The fitness function for the lac operon reads W = W0·(1 + B - C), where B is the benefit function and C is the cost function.
claims.source: Thus, the fitness function reads W = W0·(1 + B - C), where W0 is the cell growth rate in absence of lactose (x = 0).
claims.evidence: Mathematical model definition in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: The benefit function for lactose utilization is B = a·y·x / (k + x), where a accounts for the increase in growth rate due to lactose utilization.
claims.source: In this particular case, the benefit function reads B = a·y·x / (k + x), where a accounts for the increase in growth rate due to lactose utilization (x denotes its concentration; y denotes the normalized LacZ expression), and k is the Michaelis-Menten constant.
claims.evidence: Mathematical model definition in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: The cost function for LacZ expression is C = b·y / (h - y), where b accounts for the decrease in growth rate due to LacZ expression.
claims.source: In addition, the cost function reads C = b·y / (h - y), where b accounts for the decrease in growth rate due to LacZ expression, and h for the maximal resources available in the cell (Dekel and Alon, 2005).
claims.evidence: Mathematical model definition in Materials and methods, citing Dekel and Alon 2005.

claims.claim: The normalized LacZ expression in the deterministic regime is given by y = x^n/(x0^n + x^n), where x0 is the lactose regulatory constant and n is the Hill coefficient.
claims.source: Moreover, the normalized LacZ expression, in the deterministic regime, is given by y = xn/(x0n + xn), where x0 is the lactose regulatory constant, and n the Hill coefficient (accounting for the regulatory sensitivity).
claims.evidence: Mathematical model definition in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: Parameter values for the lac system model were experimentally fitted, resulting in W0 = 1 h^-1, a = 0.17, k = 0.40 mM, b = 0.036, h = 1.80, x0 = 0.13 mM, and n = 4.
claims.source: All parameter values were experimentally fitted, resulting in W0 = 1 h−1, a = 0.17, k = 0.40 mM, b = 0.036, h = 1.80, x0 = 0.13 mM, and n = 4 (Dekel and Alon, 2005).
claims.evidence: Experimental parameter values from Dekel and Alon 2005.

claims.claim: The normalized LacZ expression in presence of molecular noise is modeled as y = ymax·(x·z1·z0)^n / [x0^n + (x·z1·z0)^n], where z1 and z0 are random variables accounting for intrinsic and extrinsic noise.
claims.source: The normalized LacZ expression in presence of molecular noise was modeled, in steady state, as y = ymax·(x·z1·z0)n / [x0n + (x·z1·z0)n], where ymax is the maximal expression level (in general, ymax = 1), and z1 and z0 random variables accounting for intrinsic and extrinsic noise sources, respectively.
claims.evidence: Mathematical model definition in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: Intrinsic and extrinsic noise variables z1 and z0 are log-normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviations ηin and ηex respectively.
claims.source: Here, they were log-normally distributed [with mean 0 for both log(z1) and log(z0), and standard deviation ηin for log(z1) and ηex for log(z0)].
claims.evidence: Mathematical model specification in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: Typical values of noise magnitude (ηin and ηex) range between 0.1 and 0.5, leading to gene expression noise coefficients of variation between 0.26 and 0.72.
claims.source: Typical values characterizing the magnitude of the stochastic fluctuations (ηin and ηex) range between 0.1 and 0.5. They lead to values of gene expression noise (understood as the coefficient of variation) between 0.26 and 0.72 (in the case of ηin = ηex and x = x0), in agreement with experimental reports (Elowitz et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Model parameters validated against experimental data from Elowitz et al. 2002.

claims.claim: The combined expression of two lacZ genes is modeled with independent intrinsic noise (z1 and z2) but common extrinsic noise (z0).
claims.source: The combined expression of two genes coding for LacZ in presence of molecular noise was modeled as y = ymax,1·(x·z1·z0)n / [x0n + (x·z1·z0)n]+ymax,2·(x·z2·z0)n / [x0n + (x·z2·z0)n], where z2 is a random variable accounting for intrinsic noise on the second copy, with the same distribution as for z1 (z1 and z0 as before). Note that whilst extrinsic fluctuations (z0) are common, intrinsic fluctuations (z1 and z2) are independent for each gene copy (Elowitz et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Mathematical model for gene duplication, citing Elowitz et al. 2002 for noise independence.

claims.claim: The parameter h in the cost function was set in terms of genome size as h ≈ 0.36·G to model organisms of different complexity.
claims.source: In addition, the bacterial model was modified to simulate the effect of gene duplication in organisms of different complexity. For that, the parameter h in the cost function was set in terms of the genome size (G, in Mbp of haploid genome), simply as h ≈ 0.36·G (e.g. G ≈ 5 for E. coli, or G ≈ 3000 for H. sapiens), assuming that complex organisms have more resources to accommodate new gene expressions (Lynch and Marinov, 2015).
claims.evidence: Model extension based on assumption from Lynch and Marinov 2015.

claims.claim: The effective population size was set in terms of genome size as ⟨N⟩ ≈ 3·10^9 / G^1.44.
claims.source: The effective population size (here denoted by ⟨N⟩), determinant of the fixation of new genotypes, was also set in terms of G, resulting in ⟨N⟩ ≈ 3·109 / G1.44; an equation roughly inferred from previously reported estimates (Lynch and Conery, 2003).
claims.evidence: Empirical relationship inferred from Lynch and Conery 2003.

claims.claim: Mutual information was calculated between log(x) and y to characterize information transfer in the system.
claims.source: Mutual information (I) was used as a metric to characterize information transfer by considering the system as a communication channel between the environmental molecule (lactose) and the functional protein (enzyme, LacZ) resulting from gene expression. I was calculated as previously done (Rodrigo and Poyatos, 2016), between log(x) and y.
claims.evidence: Method description citing Rodrigo and Poyatos 2016.

claims.claim: The distribution of maximal LacZ expression upon single-point mutations was inferred from a large library of mutants analyzed by Otwinowski and Nemenman, 2013.
claims.source: According to an analysis of a large library of mutants (Kinney et al., 2010) resulting in a linear model of categorical variables (Otwinowski and Nemenman, 2013), the distribution of maximal LacZ expression upon single-point mutations was inferred.
claims.evidence: Data source from Kinney et al. 2010 and analysis by Otwinowski and Nemenman 2013.

claims.claim: In silico evolution simulations used serial dilution passages with a dilution factor of D = 100 and dilution period of 1 day.
claims.source: A medium with maximal capacity for N = 105 cells was considered, and serial dilution passages were simulated (Elena and Lenski, 2003), with a dilution factor of D = 100 (in terms of volume, with deterministic dominance). The dilution period was set to 1 d.
claims.evidence: Simulation parameters described in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: The doubling time of a cell was calculated as 1/W, where W is fitness calculated from stochastic LacZ expression.
claims.source: The doubling time of a given cell was 1/W, with W calculated from the stochastic LacZ expression.
claims.evidence: Simulation method described in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: The selection coefficient is calculated as S = W'/W - 1, where W' and W are fitness values of competing genotypes.
claims.source: In scenarios of competition between two subpopulations (i.e. two different genotypes), the ratio between them (r) reads r = r0·2S·t, where r0 is the initial ratio, S the selection coefficient, and t the time measured in generations (Hegreness et al., 2006). By setting W and W' the fitness values of each genotype (with W' > W), the selection coefficient is calculated as S = W'/W - 1.
claims.evidence: Population genetics formula from Hegreness et al. 2006.

claims.claim: The fixation probability for a beneficial mutation is Pfix = 2S.
claims.source: The fixation probability is Pfix = 2S, and the characteristic fixation time tfix = log2(⟨N⟩2)/S.
claims.evidence: Standard population genetics formula.

claims.claim: For a neutral mutant, Pfix = 1/⟨N⟩ and tfix = 2⟨N⟩.
claims.source: However, we have Pfix = 1/⟨N⟩ and tfix = 2⟨N⟩ for a neutral mutant (Kimura, 1983).
claims.evidence: Standard population genetics formula from Kimura 1983.

results.result: Gene duplication confers a weak selective advantage (~0.08-0.1%) by reducing gene expression inaccuracies from molecular noise and suboptimal regulation. This is demonstrated through stochastic simulations showing that duplicates produce more accurate responses (25% increase in mutual information) and reduce expression variance by 15-50% depending on noise type.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C25-C29 provide converging computational evidence from a well-defined mathematical model of the lac system. The stochastic simulations demonstrate noise buffering (C25, C28-C29), increased information transfer (C26), and quantified selective advantage (C27). The model parameters are based on experimental data from Dekel and Alon 2005, providing empirical grounding.

results.result: The selective advantage of gene duplication depends on environmental and noise conditions: it is maximal at intermediate lactose concentrations and high intrinsic noise levels, but decreases with extrinsic noise or high environmental variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C30-C31, C34-C36 are supported by systematic computational analysis shown in Figures 3g and 4c-e. The results logically follow from the noise buffering mechanism: intrinsic noise can be reduced by duplication while extrinsic noise affects both copies equally (C35). The intermediate lactose optimum corresponds to maximal system sensitivity (C23).

results.result: Population genetic dynamics with the mean selection coefficient accurately predicts the frequency increase of duplicates in in silico evolution experiments, demonstrating that this single parameter captures the complex stochastic evolutionary dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 and C88 are supported by in silico evolution experiments (Figure 4b) showing agreement between theoretical predictions and simulations. The validation across multiple conditions (varying noise, lactose dose, variance) strengthens this result. However, the simulations use simplified assumptions (no mutations, serial dilution) that may not fully capture natural population dynamics.

results.result: Gene duplicates undergo recurrent formation and deletion at high rates, reaching equilibrium frequencies that prevent fixation by drift under neutral conditions. In bacteria, equilibrium is reached in ~68 generations with ~0.1% frequency, while in Drosophila transient periods exceed 10^6 generations.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 are well-supported by empirical data from cited studies (Reams et al. 2010, Schrider et al. 2013) and theoretical population genetic analysis. The formation-deletion balance model (C40, Figure 5a-b) logically explains why neutral fixation is prevented (C42), contradicting conventional wisdom. The organism-specific calculations (C43, C45) follow from the empirical rates.

results.result: Most new-born duplicates with doubled expression are deleterious (selection coefficients -28% to -1%), but effectively neutral conditions can arise in higher eukaryotes due to larger genome size and smaller population size, or in bacteria at very low lactose concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 are supported by fitness calculations from the model (C50, Figure 5c-d) and population genetic principles (C54). The genome size scaling (C51-C52, C109) is based on Lynch and Marinov 2015. The effectively neutral regime at low lactose (C55) follows logically from the fitness landscape. However, the assumption of doubled expression (C48) may not always hold.

results.result: Adaptive gene duplications can arise through a two-step process: promoter mutations reducing expression by ~50% followed by duplication restoring wild-type levels. This yields a selection coefficient of 0.19% and global fixation probability of 3×10^-7 in E. coli, much higher than neutral expectations.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C65 present a novel mechanistic pathway supported by mutation distribution data (C57, C112 from Otwinowski and Nemenman 2013), mutation rate calculations (C58-C59), and fitness modeling (C60). The fixation probability calculation (C64) integrates multiple empirical parameters. However, C61-C62 note that high deletion rates in bacteria may still prevent fixation, and the calculation requires specific genetic contexts (C63).

results.result: In Drosophila melanogaster, the global fixation probability for adaptive duplicates is estimated at 10^-5, higher than neutral expectations, based on mutation rates of 5×10^-9 mut/bp/gen and the observation that complete gene duplications have little fitness impact.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 extend the bacterial analysis to Drosophila using empirical mutation rates (C66 from Schrider et al. 2013) and fitness effects (C67 from Emerson et al. 2008). The calculation follows the same logic as for bacteria. However, the fitness neutrality of duplications in Drosophila (C67) may be context-dependent.

results.result: A comprehensive model explains gene duplication fixation across organisms: higher eukaryotes can fix duplicates by drift (sector A), all organisms can fix by noise reduction if deletion rates are low (sector B), rapid environmental changes favor prokaryotes/lower eukaryotes (sector C), and prolonged changes allow fixation in any organism (sector D).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 synthesize the study's findings into a unified framework (Figure 7). The model integrates genome size, population size, deletion rates, and environmental dynamics. Each sector is supported by prior results and citations. However, C82 about novel function exploration is more speculative. The framework provides testable predictions but requires experimental validation.

results.result: Gene duplication can be positively selected as an architecture enhancing information transfer in genetic networks through noise mitigation. This is most favorable when intrinsic noise is preponderant, such as in nutrient-rich media with low expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 present the main conceptual conclusion supported by the computational results. C83 is directly demonstrated by the simulations. C84 reinterprets existing observations (Keane et al. 2014) in light of the new mechanism. C85-C87 specify conditions for intrinsic noise dominance with supporting citations. The logic is sound but relies on the model assumptions.

results.result: The theory generates testable predictions: gene expression should be maintained upon duplication (gene dosage sharing), noisy genes should be more duplicable when noise is deleterious, TATA box enrichment in duplicates reflects high noise, essential genes should be less duplicable, and local genetic context determines fixation probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C98 present testable predictions logically derived from the theory. Some predictions are supported by existing data (C90-C91 cite expression studies, C92-C93 cite yeast data, C95 connects two cited observations). Others are novel predictions (C89, C94, C96-C97). The predictions are internally consistent with the model but require direct experimental testing.

results.result: Empirical examples in E. coli and yeast show duplicates with maintained expression levels (gntK/idnK, fsaA/fsaB) and preservation of ancestral function, consistent with the noise reduction mechanism, though alternative explanations exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C75 cite empirical observations that are consistent with the theory but do not definitively prove the mechanism. C70-C71 show maintained expression in some duplicates (Qian et al. 2010, DeLuna et al. 2008). C72-C75 describe specific E. coli examples with speculation about noise reduction (C75). These are suggestive but not conclusive evidence, as other mechanisms could explain the same patterns.

results.result: The E. coli lac system exhibits a fitness trade-off where lactose provides benefit through metabolism but LacZ expression imposes cost. The actual regulation is near-optimal, with maximal sensitivity at intermediate lactose doses where information transfer is highest.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C24 characterize the model system using established knowledge (C18, C24) and experimental data from Dekel and Alon 2005 (C19-C21). The near-optimal regulation (C21-C22) is demonstrated by comparing actual and optimal dose-response curves with statistical testing (p=0.02). The sensitivity analysis (C23) is shown in Figure 1f. This provides solid foundation for the duplication analysis.

results.result: The mathematical model defines fitness as W = W0·(1 + B - C) with Michaelis-Menten benefit and resource-limited cost functions, incorporates log-normal noise distributions for intrinsic and extrinsic fluctuations, and uses standard population genetic formulas for selection and fixation.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C117 describe the mathematical framework in Materials and Methods. The fitness model (C100-C104) uses experimentally fitted parameters from Dekel and Alon 2005. The noise model (C105-C108) follows established approaches (Elowitz et al. 2002) with validated parameter ranges (C107). Population genetic formulas (C115-C117) are standard. The model is well-defined and computationally reproducible, though some simplifications are noted.

results.result: Classical theory predicts gene loss under neutrality, while existing hypotheses for positive selection include increased expression demand, functional backup for mutation accumulation, and error compensation. However, these hypotheses have limitations in explaining early-phase fixation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C17 review prior work and identify gaps in understanding. The claims accurately represent cited literature (Kimura 1983, Lynch and Conery 2000-2003, Riehle et al. 2001, etc.) and logically critique existing hypotheses (C11-C15). This establishes the motivation for the study. The characterization of prior work appears accurate based on the citations.

results.result: Genome rearrangement rates, particularly gene relocation, greatly condition duplicate fixation by reducing effective deletion rates and shifting the intrinsic-extrinsic noise balance toward more uncoupled responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C46-C47 discuss the role of genome rearrangements supported by citations (Wong and Wolfe 2005, Becskei et al. 2005). The logic is sound: relocation reduces deletion probability and increases noise independence between copies. However, the quantitative impact is not fully explored in the model, and relocation rates are mentioned but not integrated into the main calculations.

results.result: Precise experimental determination of molecular rates of gene copy number variation would reveal the extent to which natural selection has rivaled genetic drift in shaping complexity.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 proposes an important future research direction that logically follows from the study's findings. The statement is reasonable given the sensitivity of fixation probabilities to formation/deletion rates demonstrated in the results. This is a valid call for experimental work rather than a testable claim from the current study.
